payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Verifying a signature is the cheapest operation anywhere in this architecture. An Ed25519 check runs in well under a millisecond on ordinary hardware, with no network call and no vendor involved. Cost is not what stands between the industry and routine verification. The step is in nobody's job description.

The inverse of detection's problem

Detection fails on cost structure. Every item has to be evaluated, the obligation recurs forever, and the unit price never falls far enough to matter at catalog scale. Verification has the opposite profile and arrives at the same place. It is nearly free per item and almost never performed, because performing it is discretionary and no party gains by being the one who does it.

A distributor could verify at ingest, and so could a streaming service when a track enters the catalog. A rights organization could do it before registering a claim. Every one of those parties is capable, which is how the step ends up belonging to none of them.

How the web actually got to HTTPS

Certificate validation once sat in a similar position, and the sequence that resolved it is more instructive than the version usually told. The familiar story is that Chrome began marking plain HTTP as not secure in July 2018 and the web fell into line. It ran the other way. Google published its thresholds ahead of time and tied the warning to adoption, committing to mark non-secure origins only once encrypted page loads passed 75 percent, specifically so the change would not be disruptive when it landed. Chrome 68 shipped almost exactly as that line was crossed.

What carried adoption to 75 percent was cost. When Let's Encrypt entered public beta in December 2015, encrypted page loads sat near 40 percent. Free automated certificates removed the reason not to hold one, and the share climbed for two and a half years while nobody was being warned about anything. The visible failure state arrived last, as a closing move against a shrinking minority rather than as the instrument that produced compliance.

A control that only fires during a dispute

Music sits at the earlier stage of that sequence rather than the later one. Signing is not yet free and automatic at the point where work gets made, and a signed track renders identically to an unsigned one on every surface a listener or a licensing manager ever sees. Verification consequently happens after something has already gone wrong, when a claim is contested and somebody finally has a reason to look.

That timing decides how the whole thing gets funded. A control that fires only during disputes appears on a budget as legal expense avoided, which is a real number and a nearly impossible one to forecast. A control that runs at ingest appears as an operating cost with a measurable pass rate. The second is fundable. The first mostly is not, which explains a good deal of why the question keeps getting deferred to a quarter that never arrives.

Which raises a sequencing question the debate mostly skips. The visible warning and the free automatic certificate were not interchangeable moves, and on the web they arrived two and a half years apart in a fixed order, with the warning last. Whether music needs that same order is unsettled, and the evidence for it is a single company's published thresholds, from a different industry. The platforms have already worked out why they would rather not go first. Nobody has answered who will.

References

Let's Encrypt. "Public Beta: December 3, 2015." November 12, 2015. letsencrypt.org

Let's Encrypt. "Progress Towards 100% HTTPS, June 2016." June 22, 2016. letsencrypt.org

Schechter, E. "A secure web is here to stay." Google Online Security Blog, February 8, 2018. security.googleblog.com

Cloudflare. "HTTPS or bust: Chrome's plan to label sites as Not Secure." blog.cloudflare.com
